lessons.culture: In many Moroccan homes shoes come off at the door, and a guest usually brings sweets, pastries or dates rather than anything expensive. The host answers the gift with a modest "maakaansh khaaSSek" (you shouldn't have) and the guest is told he is in his own home.

too_formal.feedback: Correct but too formal-religious for a doorway welcome.

exercises.tip: "Allaah ybaarek fiik" is the set answer to "mar7baa bik".

options: Excuse me, I want to wash my hands

exercises.tip: "زوين/زوينة" is beautiful and "بزاف" is very or a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Youssef
dialogue.arabic: مرحبا بيكم، دخلو. عطيوني الجاكيطات ديالكم، نعلقهم

dialogue.speaker: Nadia

dialogue.speaker: Youssef

Your kids have grown so much!

lessons.culture: Moroccan hospitality nearly always starts with mint tea (ataay), often with a plate of sweets and pastries called l-7elwa. Refusing outright can seem cold, so guests take at least a glass and compliment the house and the children.

exercises.prompt: A host asks "قهوة ولا أتاي؟". What is he asking?
exercises.tip: "wlla" is "or" in Moroccan Arabic.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks: "كتدير السكر فالقهوة؟" and you take none. Reply.

too_formal.feedback: Correct but bookish; "blaa sukkar" is what people say.

exercises.tip: "blaa" means "without".

too_formal.feedback: Correct formal Arabic, but everyday Moroccan speech says "j-jakiTaat".

exercises.tip: "dyaalkum" means "yours (pl.)" and is used instead of MSA possessive endings.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Take your time, no rush."

lessons.culture: A Moroccan meal is often eaten from one shared dish, with bread used as the spoon and each person eating from the part nearest to them. The host keeps urging more food; guests say "bismillah" to start and "l-7amdu lillaah" at the end, and the host says "b-l-hna w sh-shfaa" as they eat.

exercises.tip: "b-l-hna w sh-shfaa" is the Moroccan "bon appetit".

dialogue.speaker: Salma

response.english: God keep you, it will be passed on.

lessons.culture: Leaving a Moroccan home takes a while: the guest announces they must go, the host insists they stay, and this can repeat several times. Guests say "Allaah y3Tiik S-S7a" for the hospitality and hosts often walk them to the door or the car.

exercises.prompt: You say you must leave and the host says "باقي بكري، بقاو شوية". Reply.

exercises.tip: "khaaSna" means "we must" and "nemshiw" is "we go".

too_formal.feedback: Correct formal Arabic, but everyday Moroccan speech says "tbeSSTna".

exercises.tip: "tbeSSTna" is "we enjoyed ourselves".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Give my regards to the family."

too_formal.feedback: Correct formal Arabic, but everyday Moroccan speech says "sellem liyya 3la".

exercises.tip: "sellem liyya 3la" means "greet for me".

exercises.prompt: What do you say when leaving a house in the evening?
exercises.tip: "teSb7u 3la khiir" to several people; "teSbe7 3la khiir" to one.

exercises.prompt: Arrange: Don't forget, our house is always your house.

too_formal.item: لا تنسوا أن بيتنا بيتكم دائما
too_formal.feedback: Correct formal Arabic, but everyday Moroccan speech says "daarna daarkum".

exercises.tip: "maa ...sh" makes a verb negative in Moroccan Arabic.

exercises.tip: Promises about the future normally include "in shaa2 Allaah".

exercises.tip: "3ayyTu" is "call" and "mli" means "when".

exercises.tip: "b-slaama" is the standard Moroccan goodbye.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "A very nice gathering, God keep you."

too_formal.feedback: Correct formal Arabic, but everyday Moroccan speech says "zwiina bzzaf".

exercises.tip: "Allaah ykhallik" is the everyday thanks.

exercises.prompt: How do you thank a host as you are leaving?
exercises.tip: "Allaah y3Tiik S-S7a" works for any hospitality.

challenge.title: Hosting or Visiting: A Full Exchange
challenge.instructions: Write a short conversation where you either welcome a guest into your home from the door to the table, or visit someone else's home and take your leave at the end. Use at least one welcome phrase, one phrase about food or drink, and one closing or thanking phrase.
required_elements: a welcome phrase at the door (e.g. mar7baa bik, dkhel tfaDDal)
an offer of food or drink (e.g. qahwa wlla ataay?)
a closing thanks or goodbye (e.g. Allaah y3Tiik S-S7a / b-slaama)
